newsitem.title: UK: BoE's George - yield curves price in EMU go-ahead.
newsitem.headline: BoE's George - yield curves price in EMU go-ahead.

text.p: Bank of England governor Eddie George said on Tuesday that French and German yield curves are positioned for European economic and monetary union going ahead.
But the steep rise in implied future yields suggests considerable uncertainty remains over EMU, he said.

"The fact that the yield curves in Germany and France are practically identical is consistent with EMU going ahead -- at least with a narrow membership," George said at the opening of the Euromoney international bond congress in London.
"But the steep rise in implied future yields five years ahead suggests that inflation is expected to be higher in the medium-term," George said.
That could reflect expectations of looser macro-economic policies, "perhaps more specifically reflecting market uncertainty about EMU," he said.

George highlighted the ongoing debate about who should join EMU an also to what extent a European Central Bank would be free to pursue its goal of price stability. "It may, on the other hand, simply reflect some kind of market imperfection," George said.

George said five-year forward yields in Italy and Spain remain much higher than in Germany and France, "suggesting that early EMU membership (for Italy and Spain) is not at all certain in the eyes of the markets."

George said the prospects for European bond markets were clouded by pressure to bring budget deficits down sufficiently to meet the Maastricht convergence criteria this year, despite the weakness of certain economies.
He said sustained expansion of demand in the United States and Britain had raised expectations of a cyclical rise in short-term interest rates.
Sluggish activity in Europe and Japan meant rates there are lower and seen less likely to rise in the short-term.

"Of course, these conclusions are based on bond markets as they currently are, which is a bit like forecasting the past," George said. "What you really need to know is how the markets will evolve in the future. Happily, it is not my task to venture down that path."
